title: Ἀνδρομάχης θρῆνος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Priam sees his son’s body dragged behind the chariot and would rush out through the Dardanian Gates to beg Achilles for it; the people hold him back, and he rolls in the dung and begs them by name to let him go, then mourns Hector above all his dead sons. Hecuba takes up the lament, and the citizens groan with her. Andromache, who has heard nothing, is weaving at her loom in the inner house and has ordered warm baths for Hector’s return. She hears the cries from the tower, drops her shuttle and runs to the wall like a madwoman. There she sees him being dragged to the ships and faints, flinging away the veil that Aphrodite gave her on her wedding day. Coming back to herself she laments: for Hector gone to Hades, for herself a widow, and above all for their small son, who will go from table to table among his father’s friends and be driven from the feast by boys whose fathers live. She ends by promising to burn Hector’s clothes, since the body that should have worn them is lying at the ships, and the women groan in answer.

sentences.t: ὣς τοῦ μὲν κεκόνιτο κάρη ἅπαν·
sentences.tr: hōs tou men kekonito karē hapan·
sentences.l: So of him indeed the head, all of it, had been covered with dust;
sentences.i: So his whole head had been covered with dust;
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the end of the dragging in the last part: the dust the body raised is on the head. ὣς … μὲν looks forward to ἣ δέ ‘but she’ in the next unit. κεκόνιτο is the pluperfect passive of κονίω ‘cover with dust’, ‘had been covered with dust’, and κάρη ἅπαν is ‘the head, all of it’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δέ νυ μήτηρ
τίλλε κόμην, ἀπὸ δὲ λιπαρὴν ἔρριψε καλύπτρην
τηλόσε, κώκυσεν δὲ μάλα μέγα παῖδ’ ἐσιδοῦσα·
sentences.tr:
hē de ny mētēr
tille komēn, apo de liparēn erripse kalyptrēn
tēlose, kōkysen de mala mega paid’ esidousa·
sentences.i: But his mother tore at her hair and flung her sleek veil far from her, and cried out very loudly when she caught sight of her son;
sentences.n: ἣ δέ answers the μέν of the last unit: the mother is Hecuba, who is named at 430. τίλλε is the imperfect of τίλλω ‘pluck, tear’ without the augment, ‘was tearing’, and κόμην is ‘hair’. ἀπὸ … ἔρριψε is ‘flung away’, with the preverb ἀπό standing apart from its verb (tmesis); καλύπτρην is a ‘veil’ and λιπαρήν is the house ‘sleek’. τηλόσε ‘to a distance, far off’ ends in the direction suffix -σε. κώκυσεν is ‘cried out’ and μάλα μέγα ‘very loudly’; παῖδ’ ἐσιδοῦσα is the aorist participle of εἰσοράω, ‘having caught sight of her son’.

sentences.t:
ᾤμωξεν δ’ ἐλεεινὰ πατὴρ φίλος, ἀμφὶ δὲ λαοὶ
κωκυτῷ τ’ εἴχοντο καὶ οἰμωγῇ κατὰ ἄστυ.
sentences.tr:
ōimōxen d’ eleeina patēr philos, amphi de laoi
kōkytōi t’ eichonto kai oimōgēi kata asty.
sentences.l:
And wailed pitiably his dear father, and around the people
were held by outcry and by wailing throughout the town.
sentences.i: His dear father wailed pitiably, and all around the people were gripped by outcry and wailing throughout the town.
sentences.n: The father is Priam; πατὴρ φίλος is ‘his dear father’. ᾤμωξεν is the aorist of οἰμώζω ‘wail’, and ἐλεεινά, neuter plural used as an adverb, is ‘pitiably’. In the second line ἀμφί is the adverb ‘around’, with λαοί ‘the people’, and εἴχοντο is the imperfect passive of ἔχω, ‘were held (gripped) by’, with the datives κωκυτῷ ‘outcry’ and οἰμωγῇ ‘wailing’. κατὰ ἄστυ is ‘throughout the town’.

sentences.t:
τῷ δὲ μάλιστ’ ἄρ’ ἔην ἐναλίγκιον ὡς εἰ ἅπασα
Ἴλιος ὀφρυόεσσα πυρὶ σμύχοιτο κατ’ ἄκρης.
sentences.tr:
tōi de malist’ ar’ eēn enalinkion hōs ei hapasa
Ilios ophryoessa pyri smychoito kat’ akrēs.
sentences.l:
To this most of all was it like, as if all
Ilios, brow-bearing, were smouldering with fire from the top down.
sentences.i: It was most of all like this, as if the whole of beetling Ilios were smouldering in fire from the top down.
sentences.n: The comparison measures the noise of grief just described. τῷ is the dative of the article, ‘to this’, and ἔην is the epic imperfect ἦν; ἐναλίγκιον ‘like’ is the predicate, and ὡς εἰ takes the optative σμύχοιτο ‘were smouldering’. ὀφρυόεσσα comes from ὀφρύς ‘brow’; of a city on its height the picture is a jutting, overhanging brow, and that sense is the usual explanation, not certain. κατ’ ἄκρης is the fixed phrase ‘from the top down’.

sentences.t:
λαοὶ μέν ῥα γέροντα μόγις ἔχον ἀσχαλόωντα
ἐξελθεῖν μεμαῶτα πυλάων Δαρδανιάων.
sentences.tr:
laoi men rha geronta mogis echon aschaloōnta
exelthein memaōta pylaōn Dardaniaōn.
sentences.l:
The people, then, with difficulty were holding the old man, chafing,
eager to go out from the Dardanian gates.
sentences.i: The people could hardly hold the old man back, chafing and eager to go out of the Dardanian gates.
sentences.n: The old man is Priam, and the people are keeping him from going out to Achilles. ἔχον is the imperfect of ἔχω without the augment, ‘were holding’; μόγις is ‘with difficulty’. ἀσχαλόωντα ‘chafing’ is the uncontracted participle of ἀσχαλάω, and μεμαῶτα ‘eager’ is the perfect participle of μαίομαι; both agree with γέροντα, the accusative of γέρων ‘old man’. ἐξελθεῖν is ‘to go out’, and Δαρδανιάων is the genitive plural of the adjective ‘Dardanian’, from the ancestor Dardanus.

sentences.t:
πάντας δ’ ἐλλιτάνευε κυλινδόμενος κατὰ κόπρον,
ἐξονομακλήδην ὀνομάζων ἄνδρα ἕκαστον·
sentences.tr:
pantas d’ ellitaneue kylindomenos kata kopron,
exonomaklēdēn onomazōn andra hekaston·
sentences.l:
And all he was entreating, rolling about in the dung,
by-name naming each man:
sentences.i: He pleaded with them all as he rolled about in the dung, calling each man by name:
sentences.n: Priam, held back, turns to begging. ἐλλιτάνευε is the imperfect of ἐλλιτανεύω ‘entreat’, so ‘kept entreating’, with πάντας ‘all’ as its object. κυλινδόμενος is the middle participle of κυλίνδω, ‘rolling himself’, and κόπρος is ‘dung’. ἐξονομακλήδην is one word, ‘by-name’, built on ὄνομα ‘name’ and καλέω ‘call’, and goes with ὀνομάζων ‘naming’; ἄνδρα ἕκαστον is ‘each man’. The colon opens his speech.

sentences.t:
σχέσθε φίλοι, καί μ’ οἶον ἐάσατε κηδόμενοί περ
ἐξελθόντα πόληος ἱκέσθ’ ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
schesthe philoi, kai m’ oion easate kēdomenoi per
exelthonta polēos hikesth’ epi nēas Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
“Hold back, friends, and me alone allow, concerned though you are,
having gone out of the city, to reach the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: “Hold back, friends, and though you are concerned for me, let me go out of the city alone and reach the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: Priam is speaking, as the mark says. σχέσθε is the aorist middle imperative of ἔχω, ‘hold yourselves back, stop’, and ἐάσατε is the aorist imperative of ἐάω ‘let, allow’. Its object is μ’ οἶον ‘me alone’, which ἐξελθόντα ‘having gone out’ (accusative, agreeing with με) and ἱκέσθ’ (ἱκέσθαι, aorist infinitive of ἱκνέομαι) ‘to reach’ complete. κηδόμενοί περ is ‘concerned though you are’, the people concerned for him, and πόληος is the epic genitive of πόλις ‘city’. The speech runs on.

sentences.t:
λίσσωμ’ ἀνέρα τοῦτον ἀτάσθαλον ὀβριμοεργόν,
ἤν πως ἡλικίην αἰδέσσεται ἠδ’ ἐλεήσῃ
γῆρας·
sentences.tr:
lissōm’ anera touton atasthalon obrimoergon,
ēn pōs hēlikiēn aidessetai ēd’ eleēsēi
gēras·
sentences.i: Let me beg this wanton man, this doer of mighty deeds, in case he will show respect to my years and have pity on my old age;
sentences.n: ἀνέρα is the epic form of ἄνδρα ‘man’, and the man is Achilles, described with ἀτάσθαλον ‘wanton’ and ὀβριμοεργόν ‘mighty-working’ (a doer of mighty deeds). λίσσωμ’ is λίσσωμαι, the present subjunctive of λίσσομαι, ‘let me beg’. ἤν πως is ‘if somehow’; αἰδέσσεται ‘will show respect to’ and ἐλεήσῃ ‘will pity’ share the objects ἡλικίην ‘age’ and γῆρας ‘old age’, both Priam’s own; ἡλικίη here is a time of life, not the ‘those of his age’ of 16.808.

sentences.t:
καὶ δέ νυ τῷ γε πατὴρ τοιόσδε τέτυκται
Πηλεύς, ὅς μιν ἔτικτε καὶ ἔτρεφε πῆμα γενέσθαι
Τρωσί·
sentences.tr:
kai de ny tōi ge patēr toiosde tetyktai
Pēleus, hos min etikte kai etrephe pēma genesthai
Trōsi·
sentences.i: For he too has a father like me, Peleus, who begot him and raised him to become a woe to the Trojans;
sentences.n: The father is Peleus, Achilles’ father, set beside Priam. καὶ δέ νυ τῷ γε is ‘and indeed for him too’, and τοιόσδε is ‘of this kind’, that is, an old man like Priam. τέτυκται is the perfect passive of τεύχω, ‘has been made, has come to be’. ἔτικτε and ἔτρεφε are imperfects, ‘begot’ and ‘was rearing’; πῆμα γενέσθαι is ‘to become a woe’, and πῆμα is the house ‘woe’.

sentences.t: μάλιστα δ’ ἐμοὶ περὶ πάντων ἄλγε’ ἔθηκε.
sentences.tr: malista d’ emoi peri pantōn alge’ ethēke.
sentences.l: and most of all on me, beyond all, pains he laid.
sentences.i: but it is on me, above all others, that he has laid pains.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 422, after the stop. μάλιστα … περὶ πάντων is ‘most of all, beyond all (others)’, with περί an adverb. ἄλγε’ is ἄλγεα ‘pains’, and ἄλγε’ ἔθηκε is ‘laid pains on’ (ἔθηκε is the aorist of τίθημι), the house phrase of 1.2.

sentences.t: τόσσους γάρ μοι παῖδας ἀπέκτανε τηλεθάοντας·
sentences.tr: tossous gar moi paidas apektane tēlethaontas·
sentences.l: For so many of my sons he killed, thriving;
sentences.i: for he killed so many sons of mine, thriving as they were;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for ‘most of all’: Priam has lost many sons to Achilles. τόσσους is ‘so many’, and ἀπέκτανε is an aorist of ἀποκτείνω ‘kill’. τηλεθάοντας ‘thriving’ is the participle of τηλεθάω, accusative plural, agreeing with παῖδας ‘sons’.

sentences.t:
τῶν πάντων οὐ τόσσον ὀδύρομαι ἀχνύμενός περ
ὡς ἑνός, οὗ μ’ ἄχος ὀξὺ κατοίσεται Ἄϊδος εἴσω,
Ἕκτορος·
sentences.tr:
tōn pantōn ou tosson odyromai achnymenos per
hōs henos, hou m’ achos oxy katoisetai Aïdos eisō,
Hektoros·
sentences.i: Of all of them I do not grieve so much, grieved as I am, as for one, on whose account sharp grief will bring me down to the house of Hades, Hector;
sentences.n: The first line stands in the same words in the Odyssey, where a man mourns Odysseus; the English of that line is reused, so ὀδύρομαι is ‘grieve’ here, where the Iliad elsewhere has ‘lament’. ὥς ἑνός is ‘as for one’, and οὗ ‘for whom’ refers back to it. ἄχος ὀξύ ‘sharp grief’ is the subject of κατοίσεται, the future of καταφέρω, ‘will carry me down’. Ἄϊδος εἴσω is ‘within Hades’, and ‘the house’ is understood; Ἄϊδος is the genitive of the older Ἄϊς (Ἀΐδαο at 482 is another form of the same name). Hector is named last.

sentences.t: ὡς ὄφελεν θανέειν ἐν χερσὶν ἐμῇσι·
sentences.tr: hōs ophelen thaneein en chersin emēisi·
sentences.l: if only he had died in my hands;
sentences.i: if only he had died in my arms;
sentences.n: ὡς ὄφελεν is a wish about the past, ‘if only he had’, here with θανέειν, the epic aorist infinitive of θνῄσκω ‘die’; ὡς is the wish-word and not ‘as’. χερσὶν ἐμῇσι is ‘in my hands’, that is, in his care, which i gives as ‘in my arms’.

sentences.t:
τώ κε κορεσσάμεθα κλαίοντέ τε μυρομένω τε
μήτηρ θ’, ἥ μιν ἔτικτε δυσάμμορος, ἠδ’ ἐγὼ αὐτός.
sentences.tr:
tō ke koressametha klaionte te myromenō te
mētēr th’, hē min etikte dysammoros, ēd’ egō autos.
sentences.l:
then we two would have had our fill, weeping and mourning,
his mother, who bore him, ill-fated, and I myself.”
sentences.i: then we would have had our fill of weeping and mourning, his mother, who bore him, ill-fated, and I myself.”
sentences.n: τώ is ‘then, in that case’. κορεσσάμεθα is the 1st plural aorist middle of κορέννυμι, ‘we would have had our fill’, with κε. κλαίοντε and μυρομένω are dual participles, ‘the two of us weeping and mourning’; the two are then named, the mother (Hecuba) and Priam himself. δυσάμμορος ‘ill-fated’ (the house rendering) agrees with μήτηρ. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατο κλαίων, ἐπὶ δὲ στενάχοντο πολῖται·
sentences.tr: hōs ephato klaiōn, epi de stenachonto politai·
sentences.l: So he spoke weeping, and groaned in answer the citizens;
sentences.i: So he spoke, weeping, and the citizens groaned in answer;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς ἔφατο is the closing formula of a speech, ‘so he spoke’. ἐπὶ δὲ στενάχοντο is ‘and groaned in answer’, with ἐπί an adverb meaning ‘in answer’; the same words close the part at 515, in the English shipped there. πολῖται are ‘citizens’.

sentences.t: Τρῳῇσιν δ’ Ἑκάβη ἁδινοῦ ἐξῆρχε γόοιο·
sentences.tr: Trōiēisin d’ Hekabē hadinou exērche gooio·
sentences.l: and to the Trojan women Hecuba led off the thronging lament:
sentences.i: and among the Trojan women Hecuba led off the thronging lament:
sentences.n: The mother is now named. Τρῳῇσιν is the dative plural of Τρῳαί ‘Trojan women’ (the epic -ῃσιν), and the dative says that they join in as she begins. ἐξῆρχε is the imperfect of ἐξάρχω ‘lead off’, which takes the genitive γόοιο, the epic genitive of γόος ‘lament’; ἁδινοῦ is the house ‘thronging’.

sentences.t:
τέκνον ἐγὼ δειλή· τί νυ βείομαι αἰνὰ παθοῦσα
σεῦ ἀποτεθνηῶτος;
sentences.tr:
teknon egō deilē· ti ny beiomai aina pathousa
seu apotethnēōtos;
sentences.l:
“Child, I miserable! Why now shall I live on, having suffered dread things,
you being dead?
sentences.i: “My child, miserable woman that I am — why am I to go on living, now that I have suffered terrible things and you are dead?
sentences.n: Hecuba is speaking, to her dead son. τέκνον is the vocative ‘child’, and ἐγὼ δειλή ‘I, miserable’ has no verb. βείομαι is the epic form of the future of βιόω ‘live’. αἰνὰ παθοῦσα is ‘having suffered dread things’ (aorist participle of πάσχω), and σεῦ ἀποτεθνηῶτος is a genitive absolute, ‘you having died’, with the perfect participle of ἀποθνῄσκω and the epic σεῦ for σοῦ.

sentences.t:
ὅ μοι νύκτάς τε καὶ ἦμαρ
εὐχωλὴ κατὰ ἄστυ πελέσκεο, πᾶσί τ’ ὄνειαρ
Τρωσί τε καὶ Τρῳῇσι κατὰ πτόλιν, οἵ σε θεὸν ὣς
δειδέχατ’·
sentences.tr:
ho moi nyktas te kai ēmar
euchōlē kata asty peleskeo, pasi t’ oneiar
Trōsi te kai Trōiēisi kata ptolin, hoi se theon hōs
deidechat’·
sentences.l:
you who for me night and day
a boast throughout the town you used to be, and for all a help,
to Trojans and to Trojan women throughout the city, who you like a god
greeted;
sentences.i: you who were my boast night and day throughout the town, and a help to all the Trojans and Trojan women throughout the city, who greeted you like a god;
sentences.n: ὅ is the neuter relative, agreeing with τέκνον (a neuter noun): ‘you who’. νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ is ‘night and day’, and πελέσκεο is the iterative imperfect of πέλομαι, ‘you used to be’. εὐχωλή is ‘a boast’, something to be proud of, and ὄνειαρ is ‘a help’. δειδέχατ’ is the elided 3rd plural past form (δειδέχατο) of the verb of welcoming, as at 4.4; with a cup it is ‘pledged’, and with no cup here it is ‘greeted’. θεὸν ὣς is ‘like a god’. The unit ends on one word of line 435.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ καί σφι μάλα μέγα κῦδος ἔησθα
ζωὸς ἐών· νῦν αὖ θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κιχάνει.
sentences.tr:
ē gar kai sphi mala mega kydos eēstha
zōos eōn· nyn au thanatos kai moira kichanei.
sentences.l:
for truly to them too very great glory you were
while living; but now death and fate overtake you.”
sentences.i: for to them, too, you were a very great glory while you lived; but now death and fate overtake you.”
sentences.n: ἦ γὰρ καί σφι is ‘for truly to them too’, and ἔησθα is the epic 2nd singular of εἰμί, ‘you were’; μάλα μέγα κῦδος is ‘very great glory’. The last line stands in the same words at 17.671 (iliad-114), where it is said of Patroclus; its English is reused with ‘you’ for ‘him’, since Hecuba is speaking to her son. κιχάνει is the present of κιχάνω ‘overtake’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατο κλαίουσ’, ἄλοχος δ’ οὔ πώ τι πέπυστο
Ἕκτορος·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephato klaious’, alochos d’ ou pō ti pepysto
Hektoros·
sentences.l:
So she spoke weeping, but the wife had not yet learned anything
of Hector;
sentences.i: So she spoke, weeping; but Hector’s wife had not yet heard anything about him;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς ἔφατο κλαίουσ’ (feminine) closes Hecuba’s speech. ἄλοχος is ‘wife’, Hector’s wife Andromache, who is not named in this part; οὔ πώ τι is ‘not yet at all’. πέπυστο is the pluperfect of πυνθάνομαι, ‘had learned’, which takes the genitive Ἕκτορος ‘about Hector’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ οἵ τις ἐτήτυμος ἄγγελος ἐλθὼν
ἤγγειλ’ ὅττί ῥά οἱ πόσις ἔκτοθι μίμνε πυλάων,
ἀλλ’ ἥ γ’ ἱστὸν ὕφαινε μυχῷ δόμου ὑψηλοῖο
δίπλακα πορφυρέην, ἐν δὲ θρόνα ποικίλ’ ἔπασσε.
sentences.tr:
ou gar hoi tis etētymos angelos elthōn
ēngeil’ hotti rha hoi posis ektothi mimne pylaōn,
all’ hē g’ histon hyphaine mychōi domou hypsēloio
diplaka porphyreēn, en de throna poikil’ epasse.
sentences.l:
for no true messenger to her, having come,
had reported that her husband was staying outside the gates,
but she was weaving a web in the inmost part of the high house,
a double cloak, purple, and in it intricate flowers she was working.
sentences.i: For no true messenger had come to tell her that her husband was staying outside the gates, but she was weaving a web in the inmost part of the high house, a double cloak of purple, and working intricate flowers into it.
sentences.n: γάρ explains why she knows nothing. ἐτήτυμος is ‘true’ and ἤγγειλ’ is the aorist of ἀγγέλλω ‘report’; ὅττι is ὅτι ‘that’, and μίμνε is the imperfect of μίμνω without the augment, ‘was staying’. ἔκτοθι πυλάων is ‘outside the gates’. ἀλλ’ ἥ γ’ ‘but she’ brings in her work: ἱστὸν ὕφαινε ‘was weaving a web’, μυχῷ δόμου ὑψηλοῖο ‘in the inmost part of the high house’, δίπλακα πορφυρέην ‘a double cloak, purple’. ἐν … ἔπασσε is ‘worked into it’ (πάσσω, tmesis). θρόνα is a rare word; ‘flowers’ is the usual explanation and the sense is not certain. ποικίλα is ‘intricate’.

sentences.t:
κέκλετο δ’ ἀμφιπόλοισιν ἐϋπλοκάμοις κατὰ δῶμα
ἀμφὶ πυρὶ στῆσαι τρίποδα μέγαν, ὄφρα πέλοιτο
Ἕκτορι θερμὰ λοετρὰ μάχης ἐκ νοστήσαντι
νηπίη,
sentences.tr:
kekleto d’ amphipoloisin eÿplokamois kata dōma
amphi pyri stēsai tripoda megan, ophra peloito
Hektori therma loetra machēs ek nostēsanti
nēpiē,
sentences.l:
she bade the fine-plaited attendants throughout the house
about the fire to set a great tripod, so that there might be
for Hector warm baths, from battle having come home,
foolish woman,
sentences.i: she told her fine-plaited attendants in the house to set a great tripod on the fire, so that there would be warm baths for Hector when he came home from battle, foolish woman,
sentences.n: Still Andromache. κέκλετο is the aorist of κέλομαι, without the augment, ‘she bade’, with the dative ἀμφιπόλοισιν ‘attendants’, ἐϋπλοκάμοις ‘fine-plaited’ and the infinitive στῆσαι ‘to set’. ὄφρα πέλοιτο is ‘so that there might be’ (optative of purpose), and θερμὰ λοετρά ‘warm baths’ means heated bath-water for Hector, μάχης ἐκ νοστήσαντι ‘come home from battle’. νηπίη ‘foolish’ is feminine and agrees with the subject; it is the poet’s pitying comment, and the clause it belongs to goes on in the next unit. The unit runs to the comma in the middle of line 445.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἐνόησεν ὅ μιν μάλα τῆλε λοετρῶν
χερσὶν Ἀχιλλῆος δάμασε γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr:
oud’ enoēsen ho min mala tēle loetrōn
chersin Achillēos damase glaukōpis Athēnē.
sentences.l:
nor did she notice that far from the baths
by the hands of Achilles gleaming-eyed Athena had subdued him.
sentences.i: and did not notice that, far from the baths, gleaming-eyed Athena had overcome him by the hands of Achilles.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 445. οὐδ’ ἐνόησεν is ‘nor did she notice’, with ὅ the conjunction ‘that’ (= ὅτι) and μιν ‘him’. μάλα τῆλε λοετρῶν is ‘very far from the baths’ (genitive of separation). δάμασε is the aorist of δαμάζω, ‘subdued’ (the house word), with γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη ‘gleaming-eyed Athena’ as subject and χερσὶν Ἀχιλλῆος ‘by the hands of Achilles’ as the means. The poet tells the reader what she does not know.

sentences.t:
κωκυτοῦ δ’ ἤκουσε καὶ οἰμωγῆς ἀπὸ πύργου·
τῆς δ’ ἐλελίχθη γυῖα, χαμαὶ δέ οἱ ἔκπεσε κερκίς·
sentences.tr:
kōkytou d’ ēkouse kai oimōgēs apo pyrgou·
tēs d’ elelichthē guia, chamai de hoi ekpese kerkis·
sentences.l:
And the outcry she heard and the wailing from the tower;
her limbs were whirled round, and to the ground fell from her the shuttle;
sentences.i: She heard the outcry and the wailing from the tower; her limbs reeled, and the shuttle fell from her to the ground;
sentences.n: She hears the lament from the tower, the one she reaches at 462. κωκυτοῦ and οἰμωγῆς are genitives after ἤκουσε ‘heard’ (the thing heard); κωκυτός is ‘outcry’ (cf. κώκυσεν at 407). τῆς is the article used as ‘her’, and ἐλελίχθη is the aorist passive of ἐλελίζω ‘whirl, shake’: her limbs (γυῖα) reel under her. χαμαί is ‘to the ground’, and οἱ ἔκπεσε ‘fell out from her’. κερκίς is a weaving tool, traditionally the shuttle; the exact tool is not certain.

sentences.t: ἣ δ’ αὖτις δμῳῇσιν ἐϋπλοκάμοισι μετηύδα·
sentences.tr: hē d’ autis dmōiēisin eÿplokamoisi metēuda·
sentences.l: and she again among her fine-plaited maidservants spoke:
sentences.i: and again she spoke among her fine-plaited maids:
sentences.n: δμῳῇσιν is the dative plural of δμῳή ‘maidservant’, the same women as the ἀμφίπολοι of 442, and ἐϋπλοκάμοισι ‘fine-plaited’ repeats the epithet. αὖτις is ‘again’ (she has already spoken to them), and μετηύδα is ‘spoke among’, the imperfect of μεταυδάω.

sentences.t: δεῦτε δύω μοι ἕπεσθον, ἴδωμ’ ὅτιν’ ἔργα τέτυκται.
sentences.tr: deute dyō moi hepesthon, idōm’ hotin’ erga tetyktai.
sentences.l: “Come, two of you, follow me, let me see what deeds have been done.
sentences.i: “Come, two of you, follow me, and let me see what has been done.
sentences.n: Andromache speaks to the maids. δεῦτε is ‘come here’, and δύω … ἕπεσθον is ‘two of you follow’, with the dual imperative of ἕπομαι. ἴδωμ’ is ἴδωμαι, the aorist subjunctive, ‘let me see’; ὅτιν’ is ὅτινα, ‘what’, a neuter plural in an indirect question, and ἔργα τέτυκται ‘deeds have been done’ has a singular verb after a neuter plural subject.

sentences.t:
αἰδοίης ἑκυρῆς ὀπὸς ἔκλυον, ἐν δ’ ἐμοὶ αὐτῇ
στήθεσι πάλλεται ἦτορ ἀνὰ στόμα, νέρθε δὲ γοῦνα
πήγνυται·
sentences.tr:
aidoiēs hekyrēs opos eklyon, en d’ emoi autēi
stēthesi palletai ētor ana stoma, nerthe de gouna
pēgnytai·
sentences.i: I heard the voice of my revered mother-in-law, and in my own breast my heart leaps up to my mouth, and below, my knees stiffen;
sentences.n: The mother-in-law is Hecuba, whose lament she has just heard. αἰδοίης is the genitive of αἰδοῖος ‘revered’, ἑκυρῆς ‘mother-in-law’ (a husband’s mother), and ὀπός ‘voice’ (genitive of ὄψ, after ἔκλυον). ἐν δ’ ἐμοὶ αὐτῇ στήθεσι is ‘and in me myself, in my breast’ (the poetic plural). πάλλεται ‘leaps’ takes ἦτορ ‘heart’ and ἀνὰ στόμα ‘up to the mouth’. γοῦνα is the epic γόνατα ‘knees’, and πήγνυται ‘are fixed, stiffen’ stands at the start of line 453, where the stop falls.

sentences.t: ἐγγὺς δή τι κακὸν Πριάμοιο τέκεσσιν.
sentences.tr: engys dē ti kakon Priamoio tekessin.
sentences.l: Near surely is some evil for the children of Priam.
sentences.i: Some evil is surely near for the children of Priam.
sentences.n: The sentence has no verb: ‘is’ is understood after ἐγγύς ‘near’. δή τι κακόν is ‘surely some evil’, and Πριάμοιο τέκεσσιν is the dative of τέκος ‘child’, ‘for Priam’s children’; Hector, her husband, is one of them.

sentences.t: αἲ γὰρ ἀπ’ οὔατος εἴη ἐμεῦ ἔπος·
sentences.tr: ai gar ap’ ouatos eiē emeu epos·
sentences.l: O if only away from the ear may my word be;
sentences.i: If only my word were away from the ear;
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ with the optative εἴη is a wish, ‘if only it might be’. ἀπ’ οὔατος is ‘away from the ear’ (οὖας, epic genitive οὔατος) and ἐμεῦ ἔπος is ‘my word’, with the epic ἐμεῦ for ἐμοῦ. The Greek does not say whose ear, and ἐμεῦ could instead go with οὔατος (‘my ear’); the sense is a wish that what she has just said should not be so.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ αἰνῶς
δείδω μὴ δή μοι θρασὺν Ἕκτορα δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
μοῦνον ἀποτμήξας πόλιος πεδίον δὲ δίηται,
sentences.tr:
alla mal’ ainōs
deidō mē dē moi thrasyn Hektora dios Achilleus
mounon apotmēxas polios pedion de diētai,
sentences.l:
but very dreadfully
I fear that for me bold Hector heavenly Achilles,
alone having cut him off from the city, may drive to the plain,
sentences.i: but I am dreadfully afraid that heavenly Achilles, having cut my bold Hector off alone from the city, may be driving him toward the plain,
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 454. δείδω μή … δίηται is a fear, ‘I fear that he may drive’, with μή and the subjunctive of δίεμαι ‘drive, chase’; μάλ’ αἰνῶς is ‘very dreadfully’. θρασύν ‘bold’ goes with Ἕκτορα, and μοι is ‘for me’. ἀποτμήξας is the aorist participle of ἀποτμήγω ‘cut off’, with μοῦνον ‘alone’ (it agrees with Ἕκτορα) and πόλιος ‘from the city’; πεδίον δέ is ‘to the plain’, with the suffix -δε of direction. She fears what the reader knows has already happened.

sentences.t:
καὶ δή μιν καταπαύσῃ ἀγηνορίης ἀλεγεινῆς
ἥ μιν ἔχεσκ’, ἐπεὶ οὔ ποτ’ ἐνὶ πληθυῖ μένεν ἀνδρῶν,
ἀλλὰ πολὺ προθέεσκε, τὸ ὃν μένος οὐδενὶ εἴκων.
sentences.tr:
kai dē min katapausēi agēnoriēs alegeinēs
hē min echesk’, epei ou pot’ eni plēthui menen andrōn,
alla poly protheeske, to hon menos oudeni eikōn.
sentences.l:
and now may make him cease from his grievous manliness
which used to hold him, since never in the throng of men would he stay,
but far ahead he would run, his own strength to no one yielding.”
sentences.i: and may now make him cease from the grievous manliness that used to hold him, since he never stayed in the throng of men, but ran far out ahead, yielding in his strength to no one.”
sentences.n: The fear continues: καὶ δή μιν καταπαύσῃ is ‘and may now make him stop’, with the genitive ἀγηνορίης (the house ‘manliness’), here ἀλεγεινῆς ‘grievous’; ἔχεσκ’ is the iterative imperfect, ‘used to hold’. The last line, and the words οὔ ποτ’ ἐνὶ πληθυῖ μένεν ἀνδρῶν in the one before it, stand in the same words in the Odyssey, and their English is reused: ἐνὶ πληθυῖ is ‘in the throng’ (dative of πληθύς), προθέεσκε ‘would run ahead’, τὸ ὃν μένος ‘his own strength’ (ὅν is the possessive), and οὐδενὶ εἴκων ‘yielding to no one’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φαμένη μεγάροιο διέσσυτο μαινάδι ἴση
παλλομένη κραδίην·
sentences.tr:
hōs phamenē megaroio diessyto mainadi isē
pallomenē kradiēn·
sentences.l:
So saying, from the hall she rushed through, like a madwoman,
leaping in heart;
sentences.i: With these words she rushed out of the hall like a madwoman, her heart leaping;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς φαμένη is ‘so saying’; μεγάροιο is ‘from the hall’, and διέσσυτο ‘rushed through’ is an aorist of διασεύομαι. μαινάδι ἴση is ‘equal to a madwoman’: μαινάς is a woman raving, the word later used of the maenads of Dionysus. παλλομένη κραδίην is ‘leaping in heart’, an accusative of respect, with the same verb as πάλλεται at 452.

sentences.t:
ἅμα δ’ ἀμφίπολοι κίον αὐτῇ
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πύργόν τε καὶ ἀνδρῶν ἷξεν ὅμιλον
ἔστη παπτήνασ’ ἐπὶ τείχεϊ, τὸν δὲ νόησεν
ἑλκόμενον πρόσθεν πόλιος·
sentences.tr:
hama d’ amphipoloi kion autēi
autar epei pyrgon te kai andrōn hixen homilon
estē paptēnas’ epi teicheï, ton de noēsen
helkomenon prosthen polios·
sentences.l:
and together the attendants went with her.
But when the tower and the throng of men she reached,
she stood, having glanced about, on the wall, and him she noticed
being dragged in front of the city;
sentences.i: and her attendants went with her. But when she reached the tower and the throng of men, she stood on the wall, glancing about, and saw him being dragged in front of the city;
sentences.n: Line 461 has no stop at its end in the edition, so the unit runs across it. ἅμα … κίον is ‘went along’ (κίον, unaugmented past of κίω). ἷξεν is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach’, and πύργον ‘tower’ and ἀνδρῶν ὅμιλον ‘throng of men’ are what she reaches. ἔστη παπτήνασ’ is ‘stood, having glanced about’ (aorist participle of παπταίνω), ἐπὶ τείχεϊ ‘on the wall’, and τὸν δὲ νόησεν ‘and she noticed him’. ἑλκόμενον is ‘being dragged’, πρόσθεν πόλιος ‘in front of the city’.

sentences.t:
ταχέες δέ μιν ἵπποι
ἕλκον ἀκηδέστως κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
tachees de min hippoi
helkon akēdestōs koilas epi nēas Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
and swift horses were dragging him uncaringly
to the hollow ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: while swift horses were dragging him uncaringly to the hollow ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 464. ταχέες ‘swift’ goes with ἵπποι ‘horses’, and ἕλκον is the imperfect ‘were dragging’. ἀκηδέστως is the adverb of ἀκηδής ‘uncaring’; the horses drag him without care for him. κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν is ‘to the hollow ships of the Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
τὴν δὲ κατ’ ὀφθαλμῶν ἐρεβεννὴ νὺξ ἐκάλυψεν,
ἤριπε δ’ ἐξοπίσω, ἀπὸ δὲ ψυχὴν ἐκάπυσσε.
sentences.tr:
tēn de kat’ ophthalmōn erebennē nyx ekalypsen,
ēripe d’ exopisō, apo de psychēn ekapysse.
sentences.l:
And her over her eyes murky night covered,
and she crashed down backward, and out of her breathed her soul.
sentences.i: Murky night covered her eyes, and she crashed down backward and breathed out her soul.
sentences.n: She faints; she does not die. τὴν δέ is ‘and her’, and κατ’ ὀφθαλμῶν ἐκάλυψεν is ‘covered down over her eyes’ (κατά with the genitive). ἐρεβεννή ‘murky’ goes with νύξ ‘night’. ἤριπε is ‘crashed down’ and ἐξοπίσω ‘backward’. ἀπὸ … ἐκάπυσσε is ‘breathed out’ (tmesis), a rare verb whose sense comes from the context, and ψυχή is the ‘soul’ that leaves in a swoon, as the revival at 475 shows.

sentences.t:
τῆλε δ’ ἀπὸ κρατὸς βάλε δέσματα σιγαλόεντα,
ἄμπυκα κεκρύφαλόν τε ἰδὲ πλεκτὴν ἀναδέσμην
κρήδεμνόν θ’,
sentences.tr:
tēle d’ apo kratos bale desmata sigaloenta,
ampyka kekryphalon te ide plektēn anadesmēn
krēdemnon th’,
sentences.l:
And far from her head she threw the glossy bindings,
frontlet and hair-net and the plaited band,
and the head-veil,
sentences.i: Far from her head she threw the glossy bindings: the frontlet, the hair-net, the plaited band, and the head-veil,
sentences.n: τῆλε is ‘far’, and ἀπὸ … βάλε is ‘threw away’ (tmesis); κρατός is the epic genitive of κάρη ‘head’. δέσματα σιγαλόεντα is ‘glossy bindings’, and the pieces are then listed: ἄμπυξ ‘frontlet’ (a band for the forehead), κεκρύφαλος ‘hair-net’ (a covering for the gathered hair), πλεκτὴ ἀναδέσμη ‘plaited band’ and κρήδεμνον ‘head-veil’. The exact shape of each is not certain. ἰδέ is the epic ‘and’. The unit ends at the comma in line 470, before the relative clause.

sentences.t:
ὅ ῥά οἱ δῶκε χρυσῆ Ἀφροδίτη
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε μιν κορυθαίολος ἠγάγεθ’ Ἕκτωρ
ἐκ δόμου Ἠετίωνος, ἐπεὶ πόρε μυρία ἕδνα.
sentences.tr:
ho rha hoi dōke chrysē Aphroditē
ēmati tōi hote min korythaiolos ēgageth’ Hektōr
ek domou Ēetiōnos, epei pore myria hedna.
sentences.l:
which to her gave golden Aphrodite
on the day when Hector of the glancing helmet led her home for himself
from the house of Eetion, after he gave countless bridal gifts.
sentences.i: which golden Aphrodite gave her on the day when Hector of the glancing helmet took her from the house of Eetion as his wife, after giving countless bridal gifts.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 470. ὅ is the relative, ‘which’, referring to the veil, and ῥά is the particle ῥα. χρυσῆ Ἀφροδίτη is ‘golden Aphrodite’. ἤματι τῷ ὅτε is ‘on the day when’. ἠγάγετο is the aorist middle of ἄγω, ‘led (her) home for himself’, that is, took her as his wife; Ἠετίωνος is the genitive of Ἠετίων, her father (480). πόρε is ‘gave’ (unaugmented aorist), and μυρία ἕδνα are ‘countless bridal gifts’, the gifts the bridegroom brings.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ μιν γαλόῳ τε καὶ εἰνατέρες ἅλις ἔσταν,
αἵ ἑ μετὰ σφίσιν εἶχον ἀτυζομένην ἀπολέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
amphi de min galoōi te kai einateres halis estan,
hai he meta sphisin eichon atyzomenēn apolesthai.
sentences.l:
And around her her husband’s two sisters and his brothers’ wives in plenty stood,
who held her among themselves, dazed with fear, to perish.
sentences.i: Around her stood her husband’s two sisters and his brothers’ wives in numbers, who held her among them, dazed with fear and close to death.
sentences.n: γαλόῳ is the dual of γάλως ‘husband’s sister’, so two of them, and εἰνατέρες are the wives of her husband’s brothers; ἔσταν is the aorist ‘stood’ (= ἔστησαν, intransitive), and ἅλις ‘in plenty’. αἵ ἑ μετὰ σφίσιν εἶχον is ‘who held her among themselves’, with ἑ ‘her’. ἀτυζομένην is ‘dazed with fear’, and ἀπολέσθαι ‘to perish’ says how far gone she was: close to dying.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν ἔμπνυτο καὶ ἐς φρένα θυμὸς ἀγέρθη
ἀμβλήδην γοόωσα μετὰ Τρῳῇσιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ epei oun empnyto kai es phrena thymos agerthē
amblēdēn gooōsa meta Trōiēisin eeipen·
sentences.l:
But she, when then she recovered breath and into her wits her spirit was gathered,
in bursts sobbing spoke among the Trojan women:
sentences.i: But when she had revived and her spirit was gathered back into her wits, she spoke among the Trojan women, sobbing in bursts:
sentences.n: ἔμπνυτο is the aorist of ἐμπνέω, ‘recovered breath, revived’, and ἐς φρένα θυμὸς ἀγέρθη is ‘her spirit was gathered into her wits’ (ἀγέρθη, aorist passive of ἀγείρω). ἀμβλήδην is an adverb of uncertain sense; ‘in bursts’ is the usual explanation, not certain. γοόωσα is the uncontracted participle ‘sobbing’, and μετὰ Τρῳῇσιν is ‘among the Trojan women’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ ἐγὼ δύστηνος· ἰῇ ἄρα γεινόμεθ’ αἴσῃ
ἀμφότεροι, σὺ μὲν ἐν Τροίῃ Πριάμου κατὰ δῶμα,
sentences.tr:
Hektor egō dystēnos· iēi ara geinometh’ aisēi
amphoteroi, sy men en Troiēi Priamou kata dōma,
sentences.l:
“Hector, I wretched! In one lot, then, we were born,
both of us, you in Troy, in the house of Priam,
sentences.i: “Hector, wretched that I am! We were both born to one lot, you in Troy in the house of Priam,
sentences.n: Andromache laments; the mark says so. ἐγὼ δύστηνος is ‘I wretched’ (δύστηνος has one form for both genders). γεινόμεθ’ is the imperfect ‘we were born’, and ἰῇ … αἴσῃ is ‘to one lot’, ἰῇ being the feminine of ‘one’. ἀμφότεροι is ‘both of us’; the sentence is carried on in the next unit with αὐτὰρ ἐγώ. Πριάμου κατὰ δῶμα is ‘in the house of Priam’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ Θήβῃσιν ὑπὸ Πλάκῳ ὑληέσσῃ
ἐν δόμῳ Ἠετίωνος, ὅ μ’ ἔτρεφε τυτθὸν ἐοῦσαν
δύσμορος αἰνόμορον· ὡς μὴ ὤφελλε τεκέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
autar egō Thēbēisin hypo Plakōi hylēessēi
en domōi Ēetiōnos, ho m’ etrephe tytthon eousan
dysmoros ainomoron· hōs mē ōphelle tekesthai.
sentences.l:
but I at Thebes beneath wooded Placus
in the house of Eetion, who reared me when I was little,
he ill-starred, me dread-fated; if only he had not begotten me.
sentences.i: and I at Thebes beneath wooded Placus, in the house of Eetion, who reared me when I was little — he ill-starred, I grimly fated; if only he had not begotten me.
sentences.n: Her father Eetion reared her at Thebe, the town below Placus. Θήβῃσιν is ‘at Thebes’ and ὑπὸ Πλάκῳ ὑληέσσῃ ‘beneath wooded Placus’. ὅ μ’ ἔτρεφε is ‘who reared me’, and τυτθὸν ἐοῦσαν ‘when I was little’. δύσμορος (nominative, Eetion) is ‘ill-starred’ and αἰνόμορον (accusative, μ’) ‘dread-fated’. ὡς μὴ ὤφελλε τεκέσθαι is a wish about the past, ‘if only he had not begotten me’, with the aorist middle infinitive of τίκτω.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ σὺ μὲν Ἀΐδαο δόμους ὑπὸ κεύθεσι γαίης
ἔρχεαι, αὐτὰρ ἐμὲ στυγερῷ ἐνὶ πένθεϊ λείπεις
χήρην ἐν μεγάροισι·
sentences.tr:
nyn de sy men Aïdao domous hypo keuthesi gaiēs
ercheai, autar eme stygerōi eni pentheï leipeis
chērēn en megaroisi·
sentences.i: And now you are going to the house of Hades beneath the hidden places of the earth, and you leave me in hateful grief, a widow in the halls;
sentences.n: νῦν δὲ σὺ μέν sets Hector’s lot against hers. Ἀΐδαο δόμους is ‘the house of Hades’ (the plural δόμους for one dwelling), and ὑπὸ κεύθεσι γαίης ‘beneath the hidden places of the earth’ (κεῦθος, dative plural). ἔρχεαι is the uncontracted 2nd singular ‘you go’. στυγερῷ ἐνὶ πένθεϊ is ‘in hateful grief’, and χήρην ‘a widow’ agrees with ἐμέ.

sentences.t:
πάϊς δ’ ἔτι νήπιος αὔτως,
ὃν τέκομεν σύ τ’ ἐγώ τε δυσάμμοροι·
sentences.tr:
païs d’ eti nēpios autōs,
hon tekomen sy t’ egō te dysammoroi·
sentences.l:
and the child still an infant, just so,
whom we brought forth, you and I, ill-fated;
sentences.i: and our son is still a mere infant, whom you and I brought forth, ill-fated that we are;
sentences.n: The child is Astyanax, who is named at 500. νήπιος here is the baby, ‘infant’ (not the ‘foolish’ of 445), and αὔτως ‘just so, merely’. ὃν τέκομεν is ‘whom we brought forth’ (aorist of τίκτω with both parents as subject), and δυσάμμοροι is the plural of the δυσάμμορος of 428, ‘ill-fated’.

sentences.t:
οὔτε σὺ τούτῳ
ἔσσεαι Ἕκτορ ὄνειαρ ἐπεὶ θάνες, οὔτε σοὶ οὗτος.
sentences.tr:
oute sy toutōi
esseai Hektor oneiar epei thanes, oute soi houtos.
sentences.l:
neither will you to him
be, Hector, a help, since you died, nor he to you.
sentences.i: You will be no help to him, Hector, since you have died, nor he to you.
sentences.n: οὔτε … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’. ἔσσεαι is the epic 2nd singular future of εἰμί, ‘you will be’, and ὄνειαρ ‘help’ is its predicate (the word of 433). ἐπεὶ θάνες is ‘since you died’ (aorist of θνῄσκω), and σοὶ οὗτος is ‘he to you’.

sentences.t:
ἤν περ γὰρ πόλεμόν γε φύγῃ πολύδακρυν Ἀχαιῶν,
αἰεί τοι τούτῳ γε πόνος καὶ κήδε’ ὀπίσσω
ἔσσοντ’·
sentences.tr:
ēn per gar polemon ge phygēi polydakryn Achaiōn,
aiei toi toutōi ge ponos kai kēde’ opissō
essont’·
sentences.i: For even if he escapes the tearful war of the Achaeans, toil and sorrows will always be his hereafter;
sentences.n: ἤν περ γάρ is ‘for even if’, and φύγῃ is the aorist subjunctive of φεύγω with πόλεμον as object, ‘escape the war’; πολύδακρυν is ‘tearful’. αἰεί τοι τούτῳ γε is ‘always, surely, for him’: τοι is the particle ‘surely’ (not ‘to you’), and τούτῳ is the child. ἔσσοντ’ is the epic future ἔσσονται, a plural verb with πόνος καὶ κήδεα; κήδεα are ‘sorrows’, and ὀπίσσω ‘hereafter’.

sentences.t: ἄλλοι γάρ οἱ ἀπουρίσσουσιν ἀρούρας.
sentences.tr: alloi gar hoi apourissousin arouras.
sentences.l: for others from him will take away the fields.
sentences.i: for others will take his fields away from him.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 489. ἀπουρίσσουσιν is a present with the sense of what is bound to happen, ‘will take away’; the verb is built on οὖρος ‘boundary’ and the picture of shifting the boundary to take land is the usual explanation, not certain. οἱ is ‘from him’, and ἀρούρας are ‘fields’ (ploughland).

sentences.t: ἦμαρ δ’ ὀρφανικὸν παναφήλικα παῖδα τίθησι·
sentences.tr: ēmar d’ orphanikon panaphēlika paida tithēsi·
sentences.l: And the orphan day a child wholly without age-mates makes;
sentences.i: The day of orphanhood leaves a child with no companions of his own age at all;
sentences.n: From here to 498 Andromache describes the life of a fatherless boy, mostly in general statements in the present tense. ἦμαρ ὀρφανικόν is ‘the orphan day’, the day of being orphaned; παναφήλικα is ‘wholly without age-mates’ (παν- ‘all’, ἀφῆλιξ ‘without those of one’s age’); τίθησι is ‘makes, puts’.

sentences.t:
πάντα δ’ ὑπεμνήμυκε, δεδάκρυνται δὲ παρειαί,
δευόμενος δέ τ’ ἄνεισι πάϊς ἐς πατρὸς ἑταίρους,
ἄλλον μὲν χλαίνης ἐρύων, ἄλλον δὲ χιτῶνος·
sentences.tr:
panta d’ hypemnēmyke, dedakryntai de pareiai,
deuomenos de t’ aneisi païs es patros hetairous,
allon men chlainēs eryōn, allon de chitōnos·
sentences.i: he is wholly downcast, and his cheeks are wet with tears, and in his need the boy goes up to his father’s companions, tugging one by the cloak, another by the tunic;
sentences.n: πάντα is ‘in every way’. ὑπεμνήμυκε is a rare perfect, ‘he is bowed down’; the sense is the usual explanation and comes mostly from the context. δεδάκρυνται is the perfect passive of δακρύω, ‘are wet with tears’, with παρειαί ‘cheeks’. δευόμενος is ‘in need’ (δεύομαι), and ἄνεισι ‘goes up’ has the epic τε of general truth. πατρὸς ἑταίρους are ‘his father’s companions’, and ἐρύων ‘tugging’ takes the genitives of the part gripped: ἄλλον μὲν χλαίνης … ἄλλον δὲ χιτῶνος, ‘one by the cloak, another by the tunic’.

sentences.t: τῶν δ’ ἐλεησάντων κοτύλην τις τυτθὸν ἐπέσχε·
sentences.tr: tōn d’ eleēsantōn kotylēn tis tytthon epesche·
sentences.l: And of those who pity, someone holds out a cup a little;
sentences.i: One of those who pity him holds out a cup for a little;
sentences.n: τῶν δ’ ἐλεησάντων is a genitive of the aorist participle, ‘of those who pity’, and the aorist ἐπέσχε ‘holds out’ states what regularly happens. κοτύλην is ‘a cup’, and τυτθόν ‘a little’ is an adverb that can mean a little time or a little quantity; the Greek does not say which.

sentences.t: χείλεα μέν τ’ ἐδίην’, ὑπερῴην δ’ οὐκ ἐδίηνε.
sentences.tr: cheilea men t’ ediēn’, hyperōiēn d’ ouk ediēne.
sentences.l: the lips it wets, but the palate it does not wet.
sentences.i: it wets his lips, but does not wet his palate.
sentences.n: The Greek names no subject for the verbs, which are again aorists stating what regularly happens: the cup is meant. ἐδίην’ is ἐδίηνε, from διαίνω ‘wet’. ὑπερῴη is ‘the palate’, the upper part of the mouth.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ καὶ ἀμφιθαλὴς ἐκ δαιτύος ἐστυφέλιξε
χερσὶν πεπλήγων καὶ ὀνειδείοισιν ἐνίσσων·
sentences.tr:
ton de kai amphithalēs ek daityos estyphelixe
chersin peplēgōn kai oneideioisin enissōn·
sentences.l:
And him, too, one flourishing on both sides from the feast thrusts roughly,
striking with his hands and with reproachful words upbraiding:
sentences.i: And him, too, a boy whose parents are both living pushes roughly away from the feast, striking him with his hands and upbraiding him with reproaches:
sentences.n: ἀμφιθαλής is ‘flourishing on both sides’, a boy whose father and mother are both alive. ἐστυφέλιξε is the aorist of στυφελίζω ‘thrust roughly’, again for what regularly happens. πεπλήγων is a participle of πλήσσω ‘strike’ (χερσίν ‘with his hands’), and ὀνειδείοισιν is the dative plural of the adjective ὀνείδειος, ‘reproachful’, used as a noun, ‘with reproaches’; ἐνίσσων is the participle of ἐνίσσω ‘upbraid’. The colon opens the boy’s words, which are inside Andromache’s speech and so take single quotation marks.

sentences.t: ἔρρ’ οὕτως· οὐ σός γε πατὴρ μεταδαίνυται ἡμῖν.
sentences.tr: err’ houtōs· ou sos ge patēr metadainytai hēmin.
sentences.l: ‘Be off, thus; no father of yours at least feasts with us.’
sentences.i: ‘Be off, just as you are; your father is not feasting with us.’
sentences.n: The boy’s words, in single marks because they lie inside Andromache’s speech. ἔρρ’ is ἔρρε, the imperative of ἔρρω ‘go with ill luck’, a curt dismissal; οὕτως is ‘thus, just as you are’. μεταδαίνυται is ‘shares the feast with’ (μετά, δαίνυμαι), with the dative ἡμῖν ‘with us’. The dead father is the point of the taunt.
sentences.mark: A boy with both parents living speaks

sentences.t:
δακρυόεις δέ τ’ ἄνεισι πάϊς ἐς μητέρα χήρην
Ἀστυάναξ, ὃς πρὶν μὲν ἑοῦ ἐπὶ γούνασι πατρὸς
μυελὸν οἶον ἔδεσκε καὶ οἰῶν πίονα δημόν·
sentences.tr:
dakryoeis de t’ aneisi païs es mētera chērēn
Astyanax, hos prin men heou epi gounasi patros
myelon oion edeske kai oiōn piona dēmon·
sentences.i: And in tears the boy goes up to his widowed mother, Astyanax, who formerly, on the knees of his own father, used to eat marrow only, and the rich fat of sheep;
sentences.n: Andromache turns from the general picture to her own son. πάϊς is ‘child’, and Ἀστυάναξ names him: Ἀστυάναξ means ‘lord of the city’ (ἄστυ, ἄναξ), and the child’s own name is Σκαμάνδριος (6.402). δακρυόεις is ‘tearful’ and ἐς μητέρα χήρην ‘to his widowed mother’. πρὶν μέν is ‘formerly’ and ἑοῦ is the possessive ‘his own’. μυελὸν οἶον is ‘marrow alone’, ἔδεσκε the iterative ‘used to eat’, and οἰῶν the genitive plural of ὄϊς ‘sheep’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅθ’ ὕπνος ἕλοι, παύσαιτό τε νηπιαχεύων,
εὕδεσκ’ ἐν λέκτροισιν ἐν ἀγκαλίδεσσι τιθήνης
εὐνῇ ἔνι μαλακῇ θαλέων ἐμπλησάμενος κῆρ·
sentences.tr:
autar hoth’ hypnos heloi, pausaito te nēpiacheuōn,
heudesk’ en lektroisin en ankalidessi tithēnēs
eunēi eni malakēi thaleōn emplēsamenos kēr·
sentences.i: and when sleep took him and he gave up his childish play, he would sleep in a bed, in his nurse’s arms, on a soft couch, his heart filled with good things;
sentences.n: ὅθ’ … ἕλοι and παύσαιτο are optatives of repeated action in the past, ‘whenever sleep took him, and he stopped’; νηπιαχεύων ‘playing the child’ is built on νηπίαχος ‘childish’. εὕδεσκε is the iterative ‘would sleep’. ἀγκαλίδεσσι is ‘arms, embrace’ and τιθήνη the ‘nurse’, and εὐνῇ ἔνι μαλακῇ is ‘on a soft couch’, with ἔνι standing after the noun. θαλέων is the genitive plural of a noun related to θάλλω ‘thrive’, ‘good things’; whether food or festivity is not certain.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἂν πολλὰ πάθῃσι φίλου ἀπὸ πατρὸς ἁμαρτὼν
Ἀστυάναξ, ὃν Τρῶες ἐπίκλησιν καλέουσιν·
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ an polla pathēisi philou apo patros hamartōn
Astyanax, hon Trōes epiklēsin kaleousin·
sentences.l:
But now he will suffer many things, having lost his dear father,
Astyanax, whom the Trojans by surname call;
sentences.i: But now he will suffer much, having lost his dear father, Astyanax, whom the Trojans call by that surname;
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ is set against πρὶν μέν above. ἂν πάθῃσι is ἄν with the subjunctive, ‘he will suffer’. ἁμαρτών is the aorist participle of ἁμαρτάνω, ‘having lost’, with φίλου ἀπὸ πατρός ‘from his dear father’. ἐπίκλησιν is ‘by surname’: Ἀστυάναξ is a name the Trojans gave him, his own being Scamandrius (6.402).

sentences.t: οἶος γάρ σφιν ἔρυσο πύλας καὶ τείχεα μακρά.
sentences.tr: oios gar sphin eryso pylas kai teichea makra.
sentences.l: for alone for them you guarded the gates and the long walls.
sentences.i: for you alone guarded the gates and the long walls for them.
sentences.n: This line gives the reason for the surname, and Andromache speaks again to Hector. οἶος is ‘alone’, σφιν ‘for them’ (the Trojans), and ἔρυσο a past tense, 2nd singular middle, of ἐρύομαι ‘guard’ (cf. εἴρυντο at 12.454). πύλας καὶ τείχεα μακρά are ‘the gates and the long walls’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ σὲ μὲν παρὰ νηυσὶ κορωνίσι νόσφι τοκήων
αἰόλαι εὐλαὶ ἔδονται, ἐπεί κε κύνες κορέσωνται
γυμνόν·
sentences.tr:
nyn de se men para nēusi korōnisi nosphi tokēōn
aiolai eulai edontai, epei ke kynes koresōntai
gymnon·
sentences.i: But now beside the curved ships, far from your parents, wriggling worms will eat you, naked, after the dogs have had their fill;
sentences.n: The scene turns back to Hector’s body at the ships. σὲ μέν is the object, and αἰόλαι εὐλαί are ‘quick-moving worms’ (αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’); ἔδονται is the future of ἔδω ‘eat’. νόσφι τοκήων is ‘apart from your parents’, and ἐπεί κε κύνες κορέσωνται ‘after the dogs have had their fill’ (κε with the aorist subjunctive). γυμνόν ‘naked’ agrees with σέ, and the stop falls after it at the start of line 510.

sentences.t:
ἀτάρ τοι εἵματ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροισι κέονται
λεπτά τε καὶ χαρίεντα τετυγμένα χερσὶ γυναικῶν.
sentences.tr:
atar toi heimat’ eni megaroisi keontai
lepta te kai charienta tetygmena chersi gynaikōn.
sentences.l:
But indeed clothes in the halls lie,
delicate and graceful, well-wrought by the hands of women.
sentences.i: But your clothes lie in the halls, delicate and graceful, well wrought by women’s hands.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 510. ἀτάρ is ‘but’, and τοι is the particle ‘indeed’, which i fills out as ‘your’ from the sense. κέονται is the epic form of κεῖνται ‘lie’, in the halls (μεγάροισι) where they are stored. λεπτά is ‘delicate’, χαρίεντα ‘graceful’ and τετυγμένα ‘well-wrought’ (perfect participle of τεύχω); χερσὶ γυναικῶν is ‘by the hands of women’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι τάδε πάντα καταφλέξω πυρὶ κηλέῳ
οὐδὲν σοί γ’ ὄφελος, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἐγκείσεαι αὐτοῖς,
ἀλλὰ πρὸς Τρώων καὶ Τρωϊάδων κλέος εἶναι.
sentences.tr:
all’ ētoi tade panta kataphlexō pyri kēleōi
ouden soi g’ ophelos, epei ouk enkeiseai autois,
alla pros Trōōn kai Trōïadōn kleos einai.
sentences.l:
but indeed all these I shall burn up in blazing fire,
no use at all to you, since you will not lie in them,
but to be glory from the Trojans and the Trojan women.”
sentences.i: But I shall burn all these in blazing fire — they are no use to you, since you will not lie in them — so that they may bring you glory from the Trojans and the Trojan women.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι is ‘but indeed’. καταφλέξω is ‘I shall burn up’, with πυρὶ κηλέῳ ‘in blazing fire’. οὐδὲν σοί γ’ ὄφελος is ‘no use at all to you’, with ὄφελος a noun (‘use’), and ἐγκείσεαι αὐτοῖς ‘you will lie in them’ is the future of ἔγκειμαι. ἀλλά … κλέος εἶναι is ‘but (that they) be glory’, an infinitive of purpose, with πρὸς Τρώων καὶ Τρωϊάδων ‘from the Trojans and the Trojan women’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατο κλαίουσ’, ἐπὶ δὲ στενάχοντο γυναῖκες.
sentences.tr: hōs ephato klaious’, epi de stenachonto gynaikes.
sentences.l: So she spoke weeping, and groaned in answer the women.
sentences.i: So she spoke, weeping, and the women groaned in answer.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the last line of Book 22. The line is the same as at 429 for the citizens, and it stands in the same words in iliad-125, where it runs on into a second line; the English is reused. ὣς ἔφατο κλαίουσ’ closes Andromache’s speech, and ἐπὶ δὲ στενάχοντο γυναῖκες is ‘and the women groaned in answer’.
